title: The one sent away (6.15)
hookLine: the mother of his son is sent back to Africa and his heart is torn; a painful passage
tomorrow: how big is God, if he isn't a body?

lines: THE ONE NOT IN THE PHOTOS.
cards: A gentle warning: this is a painful passage, and the Confessions doesn't hide it. Some families have a person who isn't in the photos anymore, and nobody says why. Augustine's book has one.

He is engaged to be married, to a girl still too young to marry. And the woman he has lived with, the mother of his son, is torn from his side as an obstacle to the marriage. Who does the book send away?
Her. And it never gives her name.

teach.b: Augustine writes his own side first. His heart, which clung to her, was torn and wounded and bleeding.
Then he gives her a single sentence. She went back to Africa, vowing to God never to know another man, and leaving their son with him. That's all the text gives her.

Some readers stop right there and say it plainly: she was wronged. She loses her home, her partner and her child, and makes a vow of her own, while he, as he admits, couldn't wait for the wedding and took another woman.
Augustine doesn't defend himself. He calls himself a slave of lust, not a lover of marriage, and says the wound didn't heal; it festered.
The book is his account, told against himself.
Hers we never hear. What it does allow is a way to read it: name the wrong without looking away, and remember her vow, made to God by a woman the story never names.

how: Catholics pray for those who have been wronged and for those who wronged them; the Church teaches the equal dignity of every person. Readers of the Confessions often discuss this passage openly as a hard part of Augustine's story.

games.q: what does “the one sent away” mean?
o: Augustine's mother, sent home from Milan
the unnamed mother of his son, sent back to Africa
a servant dismissed for stealing from the house

games.q: the one sent away — tap the pairs.
p: sent back to Africa, never named

s: this is a love story with a sad but fair ending
she loses home, partner and child to suit a marriage plan; some readers say plainly she was wronged.
the Confessions gives her one sentence and her vow
she went back to Africa vowing to God, and left their son with him.
he tells it against himself, and says the wound festered.

games.q: your history class reads a great leader's memoir, and one page shows he treated a servant badly. a classmate says it's best to skip it. what fits how Augustine's page is read?
o: name the wrong plainly, and remember the one it was done to.
skip it; one bad page shouldn't spoil a great book.
throw out the whole book; nothing in it can be trusted.
games.why: Augustine tells it against himself; readers can name the wrong without looking away and still read on.

practice: Close your eyes and hold in mind the woman this passage never names, and with her, anyone you know of who was set aside to suit someone else's plans. Keep them company in your thoughts for the length of the sit.
Catholics who pray can pray for them, by name or with no name at all.

wordCard.voice: The one sent away. In book six, the mother of Augustine's son is sent back to Africa; she makes a vow to God, and the book never gives her name.

carryVoice: Your line: she was wronged, and one sentence is enough to remember her by. Two weeks, done.
